purpose: Diagnose the cold Chrome 153 M4A-to-AIFF complete-process private-memory failure without weakening the 250 MiB gate.
browser: Google Chrome 153.0.8010.48, production build on localhost, real browser conversion
formula: peak complete Chromium process-tree private memory during conversion minus stable clean blank-Chromium process-tree private memory
validation: Each browser output was a genuine AIFF/PCM file independently probed and fully decoded by the harness; the two 800-second outputs had identical byte hashes. The 400-second fixture is diagnostic only and cannot certify the 128 MiB stress gate.
inference: The extra direct-save worker is not the dominant cold-memory allocation: OPFS also exceeded 250 MiB, and the principal renderer reached 225.99 MiB in OPFS versus 230.42 MiB later in direct save. Chrome updater.exe descendants added 13.00 MiB to the direct tree peak, but a later updater-free direct sample was still 254.88 MiB incremental. Halving output from 153.6 to 76.8 MB changed the main renderer peak only 7.29 MiB; this one-run comparison is consistent with a mostly fixed working set, not proof of size independence or a precise allocation source. Focus next on the conversion renderer/engine working set; do not exclude updater or change the baseline formula.
decision: Do not claim current Chrome 153 cold direct-save or OPFS 128 MiB AIFF acceptance. Retain the faster bounded BYOB input, seek a lower-memory engine/renderer path, then repeat three-run sessions in both destination modes.
cleanup: Three raw JSON/CSV/HTML report sets, both generated M4A sources, the new diagnostic manifest, browser profiles, and project-local temporary data were removed after compaction; the pre-existing compact 128 MiB fixture manifest was preserved. No converted copy is retained.
